title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch went upstairs with his pocket bulging from the bills the merchant had paid him three months in advance. The forest deal was finished, the money was in his pocket, the shooting had gone splendidly, and Stepan Arkadyevitch was in the cheeriest possible mood — which is exactly why he was so eager to dispel the gloom that had come over Levin. He wanted to end the day at supper as pleasantly as it had begun.
Levin was indeed out of sorts, and try as he might to be warm and welcoming to his charming guest, he couldn't shake his mood. The news that Kitty wasn't married had slowly begun to intoxicate him.

Kitty was unmarried — but ill, and ill from love for a man who had spurned her. That snub seemed to rebound somehow onto Levin himself. Vronsky had slighted her; she had slighted him, Levin. By that logic Vronsky now had grounds to look down on Levin, which made him an enemy. But Levin didn't think it through that clearly. He vaguely sensed that something in it all was insulting to him, and his irritation now had no particular target — he found fault with everything in front of him. The stupid sale of the forest, the swindle pulled on Oblonsky and concluded under his own roof, infuriated him.
"Well, all finished?" he said, meeting Stepan Arkadyevitch at the top of the stairs. "Ready for supper?"
"I wouldn't say no. The appetite I work up in the country is something else! Wonderful! Why didn't you offer Ryabinin a bite?"
"Oh, the devil with him!"
"Honestly, the way you treat the man!" said Oblonsky. "You didn't even shake his hand. Why wouldn't you shake his hand?"
"Because I don't shake hands with a waiter, and a waiter is a hundred times the better man."
"What a reactionary you are, really! What about the merging of the classes?" said Oblonsky.
"Anyone who wants to merge them is welcome — it makes me sick."
"A regular reactionary, that's what you are."
"Honestly, I've never thought about what I am. I'm Konstantin Levin, and that's all."
"And Konstantin Levin in a thoroughly bad temper," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling.
"Yes, I'm in a bad temper, and do you know why? Because — forgive me — of your idiotic sale...."
Stepan Arkadyevitch made a good-natured grimace, like someone being teased and attacked for no fault of his own.

"Come on, enough of that!" he said. "When has anyone ever sold anything without being told, the moment the deal closes, 'It was worth far more than that'? And yet when you want to sell, nobody will offer you a kopeck.... No, I see you've taken a real dislike to poor old Ryabinin."

"Maybe I have. And do you know why? You'll call me a reactionary again, or some other dreadful name — but it genuinely upsets me and angers me to see, on every side, the impoverishment of the nobility I belong to. And, in spite of the merging of the classes, I'm glad to belong to it. And their impoverishment isn't from extravagance — that would be nothing; living in good style is what's proper for noblemen; only the gentry know how to do it. The peasants around us are buying land, and I don't mind that at all. The gentleman does nothing while the peasant works and pushes the idler aside. That's how it should be. And I'm genuinely glad for the peasant. But what I do mind is watching this process of impoverishment from a kind of — I don't know what to call it — innocence. Here a Polish speculator buys a magnificent estate at half price from a young lady living in Nice. There a merchant gets three acres of land worth ten roubles as security against a loan of one rouble. Here, for no earthly reason, you've handed that scoundrel a gift of thirty thousand roubles."
"Well, what was I supposed to do? Count every tree?"
"Of course they have to be counted. You didn't count them — but Ryabinin did. Ryabinin's children will have a living and an education, while yours, perhaps, will not!"

"Forgive me, but there's something petty about this counting. We have our line of business, they have theirs, and they have to make their profit. Anyway, the thing's done, and that's that. Ah, here come the poached eggs — my favorite dish. And Agafea Mihalovna will give us that marvelous herb-brandy...."
Stepan Arkadyevitch sat down at the table and started joking with Agafea Mihalovna, swearing it had been ages since he'd tasted a dinner or supper like this one.
"Well, at least you praise it," said Agafea Mihalovna, "but as for Konstantin Dmitrievitch, give him whatever you like — a crust of bread — he'll eat it and walk off."

Try as Levin might to control himself, he stayed gloomy and silent. There was one question he wanted to put to Stepan Arkadyevitch, but he couldn't bring himself to it, couldn't find the words or the right moment. Stepan Arkadyevitch had gone downstairs to his room, undressed, washed again, and got into bed in a nightshirt with goffered frills, and Levin still lingered in his room, chattering about trivial things and not daring to ask what he wanted to know.

"It really is wonderful how they make this soap," he said, examining a piece of soap he was turning over in his hands — a piece Agafea Mihalovna had set out for the guest, though Oblonsky hadn't used it. "Just look — it's practically a work of art."

"Yes, everything has been perfected to such a pitch nowadays," said Stepan Arkadyevitch with a damp, contented yawn. "The theater, for example, and the entertainments... a-a-ah!" he yawned. "And electric light everywhere... a-a-ah!"
"Yes, the electric light," said Levin. "Yes. Oh — and where is Vronsky now?" he asked abruptly, setting down the soap.

"Vronsky?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, checking his yawn. "He's in Petersburg. He left soon after you did, and he hasn't been back to Moscow since. And do you know, Kostya, I'll tell you frankly," he went on, leaning his elbow on the table and propping his handsome ruddy face on his hand, the moist, good-natured, sleepy eyes shining like stars. "It's your own fault. You took fright at the sight of your rival. But, as I told you at the time, I couldn't say which of you had the better chance. Why didn't you fight it out? I told you then...." He yawned without opening his mouth.

"Does he know, or doesn't he, that I actually proposed?" Levin wondered, staring at him. "Yes, there's something cagey, something diplomatic in his face," and feeling himself flush, he looked Stepan Arkadyevitch full in the face without a word.

"If there was anything on her side at the time, it was nothing more than a surface attraction," Oblonsky went on. "His being such a perfect aristocrat, you understand, and his future position in society — that had an effect not so much on her as on her mother."
Levin scowled. The humiliation of his rejection stung him to the quick, as if it were a fresh wound only just received. But he was at home, and the walls of one's own home are a kind of support.

"Stop, stop," he began, cutting Oblonsky off. "You go on about his being an aristocrat. But let me ask you — what does it consist of, this aristocracy of Vronsky's or anyone else's, that lets people look down on me? You consider Vronsky an aristocrat; I don't. A man whose father crawled up from nothing by intrigue, and whose mother — God only knows whose mistress she wasn't.... No, excuse me, but I consider myself an aristocrat, and people like me, who can point back in their family history to three or four honorable generations of the highest breeding (talent and intellect, of course, are another matter), and have never curried favor with anyone, never depended on anyone for anything, like my father and my grandfather. I know plenty of such families. You think it small of me to count the trees in my forest, while you make Ryabinin a present of thirty thousand; but you get rents from your estates and God knows what else, while I don't, and so I prize what's come down to me from my ancestors or what I've earned by hard work.... We are the aristocrats, not those who can only exist by the favor of the powerful of this world, and who can be bought for twopence ha'penny."

"Well, but who are you attacking? I agree with you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch sincerely and warmly — though he was perfectly aware that in the category of those who could be bought for twopence ha'penny Levin was counting him too. Levin's heat genuinely pleased him. "Who are you attacking? Though plenty of what you say about Vronsky isn't true, I won't get into that. I'll tell you straight out — if I were you, I'd come back to Moscow with me, and...."

"No; I don't know whether you've heard about it or not, but I don't care. And I'll tell you — I made an offer and was turned down, and Katerina Alexandrovna is nothing to me now but a painful and humiliating memory."
"What on earth for? What nonsense!"

"But let's not talk about it. Please forgive me if I've been disagreeable," said Levin. Now that he had opened up, he was like he had been that morning. "You're not angry with me, Stiva? Please don't be angry," he said, and, smiling, he took his hand.

"Of course not — not in the least, and no reason to be. I'm glad we've spoken openly. And, you know, the early-morning shooting is unusually good — why not come along? I couldn't sleep tonight anyway, so I might go straight from the shoot to the station."
"Excellent."
